FIELDNOTES / AUTISM & ACCESSIBILITY

AN INTERACTIVE CONVERSATION

Same conversation.
Different conditions.

You are at a community gathering, preparing a name badge while another guest starts a conversation. Follow the exchange—and keep your task in mind.

Start with visible words. Add distractions when you are ready.

01 / 04

First impression

THE WELCOME TABLE

A conversation, a badge, and everything nearby.

Your gaze shifts between the badge, the pens, and the person speaking.

Other guest

“How are we doing?”

You

“I’m… deciding whether you mean my day or the badge.”

Other guest

“No worries. Just do the usual one.”

You

“Which badge is the usual one?”

The background sound takes the foreground.

You may be thinking…

“I’m trying to understand the instruction and finish the badge. I keep noticing the pens. Looking away may help me follow the words.”

The other guest may be thinking…

“That pause felt like disengagement. I thought ‘the usual one’ was reassuring.” They have not specified which badge they mean.

Several demands at once

An ambiguous question, a badge to prepare, background sounds, and a recurring side task compete for attention.

With support

Visible words, explicit instructions, time to respond, and permission to set side tasks aside. Eye contact is not required.

YOUR MAIN TASK · KEEP THIS IN VIEW

Prepare Mia’s name badge.

Write Mia on a blue badge for table 3.

You can complete this while following the conversation.

SIDE QUEST 01

The pens are not lined up.

It feels like another task asking for your attention.

Optional. This is not required to finish the badge.

Words

What did you miss or have to reread?

Attention

What pulled you away from the conversation?

Support

Which change helped you stay involved?

About this activity & sources

This fictional activity uses visual metaphors, not harsh audio. It is not a validated simulation of autistic perception. Experiences vary; a need to align pens is not universal and does not diagnose autism or OCD. Gaze direction alone does not tell us what a person feels or understands. Nothing you enter is saved.

Background reading: National Autistic Society · Sensory processing; Milton (2012) · The double empathy problem. Illustration: いらすとや · Terms of use. The illustration depicts a person, not a diagnosis.

講者引導 · 約 5–7 分鐘

先說明：「你正在一般聚會幫忙製作名牌，旁邊的人開始聊天。請一邊跟上對話，一邊完成 Mia 的名牌。」先不開干擾，邀請觀眾說出第一印象，再開啟兩種干擾。

聲響文字框會暫時蓋住對話，把「普通背景聲變得難以忽略」具象化；旁邊反覆出現的排筆通知，則把注意力被另一件事拉走的感覺具象化。這是設計過的比喻，不代表每位自閉症者的真實內在經驗。可以排筆，也可以暫時不處理。

第二階段討論雙方可能如何解讀停頓、眼神與模糊問句；第三階段請觀眾選擇更明確的說法。按「Add support」後維持同一項名牌任務，關掉遮蔽與通知，再比較理解及參與是否變容易。不要把這次表現當作診斷或治療成效。

收尾問：「當我以為對方不專心時，還可能漏看了哪些負擔？我能怎麼改變溝通方式或環境？」隨時按 Esc 可清除干擾。

A shared situation can contain very different demands.
